text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers on Thursday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Saving through funds has increased by almost 50 billion crowns in the first half of 1997 which is a record. Share funds have been the most popular and account for nearly 75 percent of the rise. Low interest rates and gains on the stock market are behind the change in saving habits with people moving their money from bonds and banks, an industry group said.

- Coffee prices have risen almost 50 percent since the start of the year and coffee prices in Sweden have been increased by about 35 crowns a kilo to 80 crowns. The coffee market has never been as nervous as it is now, according to Swedish food industry spokesmen.

- A government suggestion to widen membership of the bourse has been given the thumbs down from the Finance Inspectorate and the Swedish fund dealers association. They say the risks of allowing insurance companies, pension funds and other big investors on the market is too great.

- Telecoms company Ericsson is one of the winners of the "golden era" for telecommunications equipment. In the past three years Ericsson has lifted its profit from seven to 16 billion crowns despite continuing to make large investments, according to a new analysis by U.S. investment bank Salomon Brothers that has put a buy recommendation on the stock.

- Two of the 1970s and 1980s most high profile property speculators, Adam Backstrom and Magnus Lindholm, have been ordered to pay $12 million by a U.S. court to Norway's shipping magnate John Fredriksen for breaking a ship contract. Backstrom is about to move back to Sweden.

- Office supplier Esselte posted a four percent higher pre-tax profit of 308 million crowns for the first half of 1997 against market expectations of a profit of 323 million crowns. The company said the result gave hope of achieving its goal of lifting profits by 10 percent rise every year.
- Only published on Fridays during the summer.
